raw_reviewer_findings.why_it_matters: Task 1 lets pnpm install a newer 11.x. If that version changed what `userInfo: false` covers, Sentry could start inferring visitors' IP addresses and every case would still pass: the only SDK check reads `sdk.integrations`, and `dataCollection` keys left unset default to permissive. decided_findings.title: A SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN in a developer's shell turns every local build into an upload attempt
decided_findings.terms_first: SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN: the secret that lets a build upload source maps to Sentry. VERCEL_ENV: a variable Vercel sets at build time — production, preview or development; web/scripts/app-version.mjs already relies on it.
decided_findings.scenario: You (or an agent) follow your own sentry skill's advice and export SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN in your shell, so you can read Sentry's issues from the terminal. From then on, every local `pnpm build` and every end-to-end run tries to create a release and upload source maps. With that read-only token, Sentry refuses, the plan's errorHandler rethrows, and every local build and the whole e2e lane fail. With a broader token, local builds upload maps named `local` into the production project, using your credential — which the spec's "an agent may not handle the token" exists to prevent.
decided_findings.whats_wrong: The plan uses the token's presence as the only gate. The user-level sentry skill tells the owner to set exactly that variable; Playwright's webServer passes the shell's environment into its `pnpm build`.
decided_findings.proposed_fix: Gate the token on VERCEL_ENV === 'production' for all three options; keep assert-no-auth-token.mjs reading SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN directly (a leaked shell token is still worth catching); add a plan Choice (12) recording the departure from spec section 4's snippet; Task 17 Step 1 asks the owner to confirm Vercel's "Enable access to System Environment Variables" is on (the wordmark tooltip reads v0.… on production, not `local`); the README sentence names the gate.
decided_findings.why_it_works: "Only Vercel's production build uploads" becomes true by construction instead of depending on a clean shell. Vercel documents VERCEL_ENV as available at build time with the value production for production deployments.
decided_findings.new_risk: With Vercel's system variables switched off, VERCEL_ENV is unset: no maps are built, nothing uploads, nothing warns, and errorHandler never fires — production frames stay unreadable. Guards: Task 17 Step 1's check of the setting, and Step 7's readable-frame check after the first deploy. (verify-B's correction.)
decided_findings.spec_change: Yes — spec section 4's snippet gates on the token alone. If approved, record it in the NH-124 changelog entry under a "Changed by the plan review, lap 1" list.
decided_findings.drop_consequence: Drop it: a developer who exports the token for the sentry skill gets failing local builds and e2e runs, or quiet uploads into production under their credential.

raw_reviewer_findings.section: Task 1 — Install @sentry/nextjs, wrap the build (Step 4, the withSentryConfig options); echoed by Task 16's README text
raw_reviewer_findings.why_it_matters: If the owner exports SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN, every local build and every e2e run tries to create a release and upload source maps. The installed `sentry` skill tells the owner to set a variable with exactly that name, system-wide, holding a read-only API token, and Playwright 1.61.1's web server passes the shell's environment into its `pnpm build`. With that read-only token, Sentry refuses the release and `errorHandler` rethrows, so local builds and the whole e2e lane fail. With a broader token, local and agent builds upload maps as release `local` into the production project, using the owner's credential, which the spec's rule that an agent may not handle the token exists to prevent. `web/scripts/app-version.mjs` already trusts VERCEL_ENV to tell a production build from a local one. Gating the token on it makes 'only Vercel's production build uploads' true by construction, not just when the shell happens to be clean.
raw_reviewer_findings.suggested_fix: In Task 1 Step 4, read the token through a production gate and use the result for all three options: `const uploadToken = process.env.VERCEL_ENV === 'production' ? process.env.SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN : undefined;`, then `authToken: uploadToken`, `sourcemaps: { disable: !uploadToken }` and `useRunAfterProductionCompileHook: Boolean(uploadToken)`. Add a comment that Sentry's own API tooling reads the same variable name from a developer's shell. Leave `assert-no-auth-token.mjs` reading SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN as it does now. Record the change from spec section 4's snippet in the plan, as its Spec line requires.
evidence: Only Vercel's Production environment holds SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN, so previews, CI and local builds upload nothing
previews, CI and local builds have neither, so they send nothing and upload nothing
Expected: PASS, with nothing printed by the new step (no token, nothing to check).

Spiked during triage: the production bundle (deployed 2026-10-04) carries the version v0.26.10.04-0821.2f83752, which app-version.mjs prints only when VERCEL_ENV is production at build time, so R-1's precondition holds today. decided_findings.title: A production build with the token but no project slug deploys with unreadable frames, silently
decided_findings.terms_first: Slug: the short name Sentry gives an organization or project (not secret). Choice 2 leaves `org` and `project` out of next.config.ts until the owner has them.
decided_findings.scenario: You add SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN to Vercel (as the registry row F7-sentry asks, before the code merges), but next.config.ts still has no `project` slug. The production build passes; Sentry's plugin only warns "No project provided. Will not upload source maps", builds the maps anyway and deletes them. Every production error then shows minified frames — exactly the outcome the owner rejected when choosing "a failed upload stops the deploy".
decided_findings.whats_wrong: errorHandler fires only on a thrown error; a missing project is a warning and a quiet return (canUploadSourceMaps and createRelease in build-plugin-manager). Task 17 Step 2 — committing the slugs first — is the only guard, and it is a person remembering an order.

before_after.where: Task 1 Step 4, web/next.config.ts (the options object moves into a named const sentryBuildOptions so it can be checked)

decided_findings.proposed_fix: In next.config.ts, name the options object, and throw when an upload token is present (after PF-7, a production build with the token) but org or project is missing. Choice 2 and Task 17 Step 2 say the build now enforces the order.
decided_findings.why_it_works: The spec chose a failing deploy over a silent one; this extends that choice to the one silent path errorHandler cannot see. A missing slug becomes a red production build with a message saying what to set.
decided_findings.depends_on: Written against PF-7's uploadToken. Without PF-7, the same check reads process.env.SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN.
decided_findings.drop_consequence: Drop it: if the token reaches Vercel before the slugs reach the code, production deploys succeed with unreadable stack traces, and nothing says so until someone opens an issue.

decided_findings.kind: decision (the plan's open question Q8, with security-lens's recommendation)
decided_findings.section: Questions the spec left to the plan — Q8; Task 5 (reportError's file context)
decided_findings.title: The exact byte count can identify a well-known file
decided_findings.scenario: A visitor downloads a popular tab file from a big tab site — thousands of people have the same file, byte for byte — and it fails to open. The report says gp5 and, say, 48,213 bytes, and Sentry keeps it for 30 days. The name never leaves the device, but someone who knows that site could match the exact size and work out which song it was.
decided_findings.whats_wrong: The spec sends "a size in bytes" — exact. The extension plus an exact size is close to a unique key for a widely shared file.

before_after.where: Task 5 reportError, one place every report passes through; tests change 31→32, 5→8, 29→32
before_after.after: file: { type: 'gp5', bytes: 65536 } — rounded up to the next power of two (0 stays 0)

options.label: 1 — Round up to the next power of two (recommended by security-lens)
options.pros: One line in reportError, no call site changes; still tells empty, tiny, ordinary and over-the-limit apart; the home copy's "type and size" stays true
options.cons: Loses exact sizes, which nothing uses today

options.label: 2 — Keep exact bytes (the spec)
options.cons: An exact size plus the type can point at one known file

options.label: 3 — Named buckets (e.g. under 16 KB, under 256 KB, under 1 MB, under 25 MB, over)
options.cons: A table to keep in step with the 25 MB limit

decided_findings.recommendation: 1 — the same protection as buckets for one line of code. Flip to 2 if exact sizes ever turn out to be needed to tell two importer failures apart.
decided_findings.spec_change: Yes — "a size in bytes" becomes a rounded size; record it in the changelog entry if chosen.

raw_reviewer_findings.title: Exact byte count fingerprints the file (Q8)
raw_reviewer_findings.section: Left open for the plan review — Lap 2's Q8, the file size (sent by Task 5's reportError)
raw_reviewer_findings.why_it_matters: A report with the file name removed can still say which song failed to open. An exact byte count plus the extension is close to a unique key for a tab file that many visitors download from the same site. These reports are kept for 30 days and can only be deleted as a whole issue. For E101–E103 and E105, the useful distinctions are empty, tiny, ordinary and over the limit, and a coarse size keeps all four. Rounding once inside reportError, which every report passes through, needs no change at the call sites, and the home page's 'the file's type and size' stays true.
raw_reviewer_findings.suggested_fix: Round the size inside reportError before it is sent: `contexts.file.bytes` becomes the next power of two at or above the real size (0 stays 0). Update the expected sizes in report.test.ts (31 → 32), OpenFileControl.test.tsx (5 → 8) and end-to-end case 2 (29 → 32).
evidence: The spec sends the exact byte count. An exact size and the extension together could identify a well-known downloaded tab file. Option: round it into ranges.
